name: Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign
label: Welcome Sign
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas Sign' (5 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1485974042: the OpenStreetMap point 'Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas Sign'.
notes: The classic roadside sign at the south end of the Strip.

text.description: The Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign is one of the best-known landmarks in the city, and it is easy to see why people queue for it. It is a 25-foot, diamond-shaped roadside sign in 1950s style, edged with flashing yellow bulbs. Silver-dollar circles spell out "Welcome" across the top, and a red eight-pointed star crowns it. Designer Betty Willis created it for Clark County, and it went up in 1959. It stands in the median of Las Vegas Boulevard South, and some consider it to be the southern end of the Strip. Many people photograph the south face, which carries the "Las Vegas" lettering. The back, which reads "Drive Carefully, Come Back Soon", is photographed far less often and usually has no queue. Since 2008 there has been official access with a small car park and a paved walkway, and since 2015 marked crosswalks, so please use those rather than crossing the road. For a phone photo, the straight-on shot is the classic, but it often has a line of people in front. Stand a little to one side, off the central line, and the sign appears at an angle with its bulbs and poles in the foreground and the sky or the Strip behind. The default lens (1x) gives the most natural look, while the ultra-wide (0.5x) fits the whole sign when the plaza is crowded. Check the edges of the frame for strangers before you press the shutter.
text.geographic_location: The sign sits in the middle of Las Vegas Boulevard South, at what some consider the southern end of the Strip. It is in Paradise, roughly 4 miles (6.4 km) south of the city limits of Las Vegas. It is north of the old stone pillars of the former McCarran Field and level with the Bali Hai Golf Club.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar public transport stops are listed for this spot. The sign's car park on Las Vegas Boulevard South can be entered only from the southbound direction, so northbound drivers may need a U-turn. Once there, use the paved walkway and the marked crosswalks to reach the sign. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the sign. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or want the poles, star and sky all in the frame. A little telephoto zoom (2x) can help you crop out other visitors.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a quieter, more dynamic picture, move to either side of the sign, off the central line, towards the north or south edge of the platform. From there you see the sign at an angle, with its bulbs and poles in the foreground and the Strip or sky behind, and fewer people queuing in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and tilt the phone slightly upwards so the sign sits in the upper two thirds of the frame, with the poles running parallel to the lines. The straight-on view of the full face, with its starburst and lettering, is the classic shot if you can wait for a gap. For something different, walk round to the back of the sign for the "Drive Carefully, Come Back Soon" lettering, which rarely has a queue.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sign to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the bulbs and neon keep their colour instead of washing out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing. Try a Live Photo to catch the bulbs flashing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The lit bulbs and neon show up better as the light fades.

text.access_note: The sign is in a public median with a small car park and marked crosswalks; use only those, never the traffic lanes, and check the official site before you go for any current restrictions.

name: Caesars Palace
label: Caesars Palace
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Las Vegas Boulevard' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Flamingo Road and Las Vegas Boulevard (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/115672893: large area 'Caesars Palace Hotel and Casino' (618 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Roman-themed resort with statues and fountains.

text.description:
Caesars Palace is one of the Strip's best-known landmarks, a big Roman-themed resort on the west side of Las Vegas Boulevard, next to Bellagio. It opened in 1966 and was built to make guests feel like emperors. That is why the name has no apostrophe: every guest is a Caesar. Statues, columns and classical details run through the property, including a 20-foot (6.1 m) statue of Augustus Caesar near the entrance. By 2016 it had 3,960 rooms in six towers, so it is far too big to fit into one frame.

For a phone photo, the easiest approach is to stay outside on the Strip sidewalk. The corner with the Roman-style gazebo gives you a framed view of the pavement and Las Vegas Boulevard, with the hotel's front grounds behind you. It is calmer than the busy lobby. The fountains out front also have a bit of history: in 1967 the stunt rider Evel Knievel tried to jump them on a motorbike.

The gazebo corner can fall into shade quickly, so check your shadows and brighten them when you edit. Inside, the Forum Shops are crowded and the painted ceilings are hard to photograph. Ask staff before taking photos in the casino. Keep your phone close to your body on the busy pavement.
text.geographic_location: Caesars Palace is on the west side of the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise, Nevada, between Bellagio and the Hard Rock site.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. From there the main hotel is about 380 m to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the gazebo corner, so you can fit the gazebo, the sidewalk and the boulevard into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as statues or the fountains.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Flamingo Road and Las Vegas Boulevard (gazebo in the far corner, out front of the hotel on the Strip sidewalk). The Strip sidewalk and Las Vegas Boulevard, framed by the gazebo, with the hotel's front grounds behind you. The main hotel complex lies to the north-west of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the gazebo up on one side of the frame, with the pavement leading into the picture. Take a second shot turned round to catch the hotel's front grounds. For another view, try the Caesars Palace Fountains, where the three lit fountains sit in front of the casino with the hotel facade rising behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the gazebo or a person, then use the exposure slider to stop the sky washing out. This corner can get shady quickly, so brighten the shadows when you edit. In the evening, switch on night mode and hold still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the pavement is quieter if you want a clean frame. Come after dark if you want the lights and fountains in the picture.

text.access_note: The Strip sidewalk is public, but the hotel, casino, pool and shops are private: the pool is for hotel guests or paying visitors, and you should ask staff before photographing inside the casino, so check the official site before you go.

name: Sphere (venue)
label: Sphere
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'LINQ Promenade' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of LINQ Promenade nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/976405284: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sphere' (247 m across).
notes: Giant LED-covered dome.

text.description:
Sphere is a huge domed entertainment venue just off the Las Vegas Strip, and its outside is the draw for photographers. The dome is covered in LED panels, so it can look like a giant moon, an eyeball or a glowing planet, depending on what is playing. It stands 366 feet (112 m) high and 516 feet (157 m) wide, and its exterior carries 580,000 sq ft of LED displays, the largest in the world. It opened on 29 September 2023 with a U2 residency, and the lit outer shell can be seen from several miles away.

From across Las Vegas Boulevard from LINQ Promenade you get a wide view of the whole sphere with neon signs in the foreground. That helps the picture feel like Las Vegas rather than just a glowing ball. Viewing from here is free and open at all hours. Sunset to about 9 PM is the best window, when the sky still has some colour and the screen is bright. The outside programming changes through the day and night, so the display you hope for may not appear. If you have time, the Sands Avenue pedestrian bridge gives a nearly head-on silhouette of the whole dome with sky behind it. The Sands Avenue bridge and its corner are on busy pavements, so step aside from the flow of people before you stop to shoot.
text.geographic_location: Sphere is in Paradise, Nevada, on the east side of the Las Vegas Strip, just east of the Venetian resort.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stops are listed for this spot. It is on the Strip and can be reached on foot. Cross Las Vegas Boulevard only at the marked crossings. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole dome with the neon signs in front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowd or buildings force you to stand close. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the screen, keeping your arms steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on LINQ Promenade (across Las Vegas Boulevard from the promenade, facing the Sphere). A wide shot of the full spherical Exosphere with neon signage in the foreground for context.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the dome in the upper-middle of the frame, with the neon signs along the bottom. Keep the phone level so the horizon and buildings stay straight. For a different angle, the Sands Avenue pedestrian bridge gives a clear head-on silhouette of the dome with the sky behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the dome to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright LED picture keeps its colours and detail. In low light, night mode can help with the street and signs. Hold the phone very still, since moving images on the dome can blur. Take a few shots, because the display changes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset to about 9 PM is the best window. The sky still has some colour and the dome's display shows up well.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from public pavement, free and at any hour, but entry to Sphere shows needs a ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Flamingo Las Vegas
label: Flamingo
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Caesars Palace' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Caesars Palace Hotel and Casino' (way/115672893): edge nearest the subject (617 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/116761428: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Flamingo Las Vegas' (305 m across).
notes: Historic pink-neon resort on the Strip.

text.description:
The Flamingo is a casino hotel on the Las Vegas Strip, and its pink neon sign and feather-topped corner are the reason people stop to photograph it. It opened its casino on 26 December 1946 and is the oldest continuously operating resort on the Strip. The original three-storey hotel was demolished in 1993, and today's building is a 28-storey tower with 3,460 rooms. Part of the grounds became a 15-acre pool area with an animal habitat that includes flamingos.

The classic view is from the Strip sidewalk directly across from the hotel, in front of Caesars Palace. From there you look east across the street and can fit the pink lights and the corner of the building into one frame. Pavements here can be busy, so take your time and keep your phone in front of you rather than stepping back into people.

If you want a second angle, the gazebo at the corner of Flamingo Road and Las Vegas Boulevard South shows the corner facade and signage up close. The flamingo habitat inside the hotel is another option for a different kind of photo, but it can be limited or closed on some days, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Flamingo is on the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise, Nevada, on the opposite side of the Strip from Caesars Palace.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or station stops at this spot. The hotel lies about 170 m to the east of that point. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the sign and the hotel front as you see them. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the pink sign and the feathered corner and leave out the traffic. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole frontage, but expect the edges to stretch and the building to look smaller.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Caesars Palace (Strip sidewalk directly across from the Flamingo, in front of Caesars). The Flamingo's pink neon sign and feather-topped corner, seen across the Strip from in front of Caesars.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the sign on one of the upper thirds, with the corner of the building filling the other side. Keep your phone level so the tower does not lean. For a closer, more angled view of the corner and signage, try the gazebo at the Flamingo Road and Las Vegas Boulevard South corner.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sign to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the pink neon keeps its colour rather than turning white. At night, let night mode run and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid support. Wait for a gap in the passing traffic if you want clean light trails or a clear view.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dusk, when the neon is lit and the sky is darker. Daytime works for seeing the building's shape, but the sign has less impact.

text.access_note: The Strip sidewalk is open public space, but the hotel and its flamingo habitat are on private property and may have changed rules, so check the official site before you go.

name: New York-New York Hotel and Casino
label: New York-New York
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue intersection' (3 web pages); placed at crossing of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/115661793: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'New York New York Hotel and Casino' (308 m across).
notes: Skyline replica with a Statue of Liberty and roller coaster.

text.description:
New York-New York is a casino hotel on the Las Vegas Strip that plays at being Manhattan. Its tower is built as a cluster of skyscrapers, with smaller replicas of city landmarks around it, including the Statue of Liberty. The tallest part is an Empire State Building replica of 47 storeys, 529 feet (161 m) high. When the hotel opened on 3 January 1997, that made it the tallest building in Nevada, until Wynn Las Vegas was finished in 2005. The Big Apple Coaster travels around the tower, so there is often something moving in your frame.

It photographs well because the whole skyline is packed into one long frontage, with plenty of colour and detail. Standing at the Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue intersection, across from the hotel's front, you can fit the full casino front into a single shot. From the lawn area you may also catch the Las Vegas Boulevard sign. At night the traffic on the boulevard adds streaks of light in front of the lit towers.

If you want a different view, try the pedestrian bridge over Las Vegas Boulevard, which frames the skyline with the Strip behind it. The pavement beside Excalibur, looking back at the hotel, puts the Excalibur towers close by. The lawn across from the hotel may be under construction, so the corner may be restricted. Have a backup spot in mind and check on site.
text.geographic_location: On the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise, Nevada. It sits on the north-west corner of the Tropicana Avenue and Las Vegas Boulevard junction, close to the MGM Grand, Excalibur and the Tropicana site.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground or tram stops at this spot, so head for the Las Vegas Strip at the Tropicana Avenue and Las Vegas Boulevard junction. Get out near that corner, then look north-west to see the hotel front. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the junction to fit the whole casino front in one frame. If you have to stand close, on a pavement or the bridge, switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to keep the towers from being cut off. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the Empire State Building replica or the Statue of Liberty.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue (across the intersection from the hotel's front). The whole casino front in one frame, with the Las Vegas Boulevard sign in view when shooting from the lawn area. The corner may be fenced off because of building work, so check on site. If it is, use the pedestrian bridge or the Excalibur-side pavement instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the vertical lines of the towers straight, so the buildings don't lean. Leave a little road or sky around the hotel rather than cropping tight. At night, include the road in the lower third so the passing traffic makes light trails. For a different view, the pedestrian bridge frames the skyline with the Strip behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lit towers to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights don't burn out. At night use night mode and brace your elbows on something solid, as it needs a steady hand for a second or two.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Night, when the traffic makes light trails in front of the lit hotel.

text.access_note: You can view the hotel from the surrounding streets, but the corner and lawn across from it may be restricted by construction, so check on site before you go.

sources.title: New York-New York Hotel and Casino

name: MGM Grand Las Vegas
label: MGM Grand
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue' (4 web pages); placed at crossing of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/116770006: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Hotel MGM Grand Las Vegas' (592 m across).
notes: Large green resort with a lion statue.

text.description: The MGM Grand is one of the biggest hotels on the Las Vegas Strip, and the best-known street-level view of it is the giant gold lion statue at the corner of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue. It photographs well because the lion, the long hotel frontage and the Strip traffic all fit into one frame, so you get a clear sense of scale and of the place. The hotel opened on 18 December 1993 and, with more than 5,000 rooms, was the largest hotel in the world at that time. Most of the building is 30 storeys high, which is why it looks so wide and tall from the pavement. Its first theme was The Wizard of Oz, but most of that was removed in a big renovation that began in 1996. Face it and put the lion in the foreground, with the Strip running behind it. Stand across the intersection from the lion so you can fit in the whole front. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the tall building doesn't lean. Pavements here can get busy, so wait for a gap in the crowd, or come early or late in the day. Take a few frames with different lenses before you move on.
text.geographic_location: The MGM Grand is near the southern end of the Las Vegas Strip, at the Tropicana Avenue and Las Vegas Boulevard intersection.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or rail stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue intersection, near the southern end of the Las Vegas Strip. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the lion and the full hotel front into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a closer shot of the lion's face.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue (sidewalk corner across the intersection from the lion, with the Strip running behind). The MGM Grand's giant gold lion statue and the hotel's front, framed against the Strip traffic at the intersection.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the phone upright so the tall building stays straight. Put the lion in the lower part of the frame and let the hotel rise behind it, with the Strip running through the background. Wait for a gap in the crowd before you take the shot. For a tighter second shot, zoom in on the lion with the telephoto lens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the lion to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and the bright building keep their detail. If you shoot after dark, let night mode do its work and hold the phone still against your body or a solid surface until it finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early or late in the day usually means fewer people on the pavement. After dark the Strip lights add colour to the background.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is a public sidewalk corner, but check the official site before you go for anything inside the resort.
claims_not_in_sources: The sidewalk at this corner can be crowded, and early or late in the day is usually quieter.
The Strip lights make the background colourful after dark, and night mode helps in low light.
The ultra-wide lens helps fit the lion and the whole hotel frontage into one frame from the corner.
Keeping the phone level and using gridlines reduces the look of the building leaning.

name: Wynn Las Vegas
label: Wynn Las Vegas
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fashion Show Footbridge' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Fashion Show Drive' (roads).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q1309059: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Bronze-glass resort tower at the north Strip.

text.description:
Wynn Las Vegas is a luxury resort on the Strip, opened on 28 April 2005 on the site of the old Desert Inn, which dated from 1950. When it opened, its 45-storey hotel tower was the tallest building in Nevada. Its sister resort, Encore, followed in December 2008 directly to the north, so from a distance the two towers sit together on the skyline. The resort's name is also written in illuminated lettering along the top of the main tower, which gives you a clear subject after dark.

The best view for a phone is from the pedestrian bridge over Las Vegas Boulevard that links the Wynn with Fashion Show Mall (often called the Fashion Show Footbridge). Check it on the map before you go. From up there you look down on the Strip's traffic and across to the Wynn and Encore towers. That gives you a sense of scale that you can't get from the pavement. The bridge is a free public walkway, but check that it is open and that nothing has changed before you go.

Stand at the middle of the bridge, face the resort and let the road lead the eye towards the towers. If you want a second picture, the lake at the resort, surrounded by the artificial mountain, is the setting for the Lake of Dreams show. It is a good place for reflections with the resort lit up behind. Check the map for its exact position.
text.geographic_location: Wynn Las Vegas stands on the Las Vegas Strip, in Paradise, Nevada, with Encore directly to its north.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stop is listed for this spot, so use a taxi or walk to the Strip near Fashion Show Mall. The footbridge crosses Las Vegas Boulevard between the mall and the Wynn. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the road, the bridge and both towers. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to fill the frame with the Wynn and Encore. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of the Strip in the picture, as it makes the towers look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Fashion Show Footbridge (pedestrian bridge over Las Vegas Blvd linking the Wynn with Fashion Show Mall). The Wynn and Encore towers seen from above the Strip, with the boulevard traffic below.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the towers on one of the vertical lines, with the road running into the lower part of the frame. Hold your phone just above the railing or glass so it doesn't show. Lake of Dreams is a good second shot if you have time, with the waterfall and lake reflections behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the lit towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright lights don't wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on the rail to keep the picture sharp. Traffic below will blur in a long exposure, which can look good.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening and after dark, when the lit resort lettering and the Strip's lights show up well.

text.access_note: The footbridge is a free public walkway, but check the official site or the signs on site before you go, as access can change.

name: Paris Las Vegas
label: Paris Eiffel Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Las Vegas Boulevard' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Paris Las Vegas'.
notes: Half-scale Eiffel Tower replica on the Strip.

text.description:
Paris Las Vegas squeezes a little of the French capital onto the Strip. The star is a half-scale Eiffel Tower, 540 feet (about 165 m) tall, with one of its four legs standing outside along the pavement and the other three inside the casino. Behind it is a stylised facade with copies of the Arc de Triomphe (two-thirds scale), the Louvre, the Paris Opera House and the Musée d'Orsay. A big hot-air balloon sign, 75 feet across, hangs out front. The resort opened on 1 September 1999 and stands on 24 acres.

It photographs well because everything is arranged to be seen from the street. The tower gives you a strong vertical line, and the facade gives you detail and colour. From the pavement opposite, the Bellagio lake and fountains sit in the foreground, so a single frame holds both. Dave Suder, who worked on the facade, said the buildings were stylised and resized to fit the site rather than copied exactly, which is why the whole group looks so tidy in a picture.

For a phone shot, take one wide frame to show the tower with the lake and fountains, then a closer one of the tower top or the balloon sign. Keep the phone level so the tower does not lean, and leave a little space above the spire. The view works by day and at night, so it is worth coming back once the lights are on.
text.geographic_location: Paris Las Vegas is on the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise, Nevada, directly south of the Horseshoe resort and connected to Bally's. The best view is from the opposite side of the Strip, by the Bellagio.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Bellagio area of the Strip. Walk to the pavement of Las Vegas Boulevard directly across from Paris, on the Bellagio side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tower, the facade and the fountain lake into one frame. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the top of the tower or the balloon sign.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Las Vegas Boulevard (sidewalk directly across the Strip from Paris Las Vegas, Bellagio side). The half-scale Eiffel Tower and the Paris facade, with the Bellagio fountains and lake in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the tower on a vertical line so it stands straight, with the lake along the bottom third. Keep other people's heads out of the foreground by waiting a moment or holding the phone slightly higher. For a different angle, try Bellagio Drive, which puts the fountains in front of the tower, but keep to the pavement because it is an active driveway. Terrazza di Sogno is another option, giving a high view over the lake, but check that it is open to the public.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and lights do not wash out. At night, let night mode run and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body until it finishes. A Live Photo can catch the fountains moving.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime and night both work. The fountain show runs to a schedule that varies by day, so check times before you go.

text.access_note: The view from the Strip pavement is of the outside of the resort, but the tower's observation deck and anything inside are separate attractions, so check the official site before you go.

name: Mandalay Bay
label: Mandalay Bay
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Las Vegas Boulevard' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/116660358: large area 'Mandalay Bay' (621 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Golden resort at the south end of the Strip.

text.description:
Mandalay Bay is the big gold-glass resort at the southern end of the Las Vegas Strip. Its 43-storey tower is the main shape you will be photographing. The resort opened on 2 March 1999 on the site of the old Hacienda hotel-casino, and it takes its name from the city of Mandalay in Myanmar, with a tropical South Seas theme to match. It covers 120 acres and has 3,209 rooms. A Four Seasons hotel occupies part of the tower, on floors 35 to 39.

It photographs well because the tower is tall, simple and clean-lined, so it fills a frame with very little clutter. The classic picture is the full height of the gold tower seen straight on from Las Vegas Boulevard, directly across from the main entrance. Stand there and the whole building fits in, with the sky above it. A second tower stands beside it, and a diagonal view along the length of the building from the corner of Las Vegas Boulevard and Hacienda Avenue shows the two together. If you fancy something different, the Welcome sign, about 0.7 miles south of the resort, is another option. Zoomed in, it makes a foreground for the gold glass behind it.

The road here is wide and busy, so take your photos from the pavement and use crosswalks only. Go in the last hour of daylight if you can, when the glass turns warmer in colour.
text.geographic_location: At the far southern end of the Las Vegas Strip, in Paradise, with Allegiant Stadium a little to the west. The address is 3950 Las Vegas Boulevard South.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station stop is listed for this spot, so the simplest way is to get to the south end of the Strip and head for the main entrance of Mandalay Bay. If you are walking along the Strip, head south until the gold tower fills your view, then use a crosswalk rather than crossing the road. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from across the road, which fits the whole tower in with some sky around it. If you are too close, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to keep the full height in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Welcome sign shot, or to pick out the gold glass pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Las Vegas Boulevard (west sidewalk, directly across from the main entrance; cross to the median if traffic allows). The full height of the gold tower straight on, with the building filling the frame. The resort lies to the west of you. Cross only at the crosswalks, and keep to the pavement or median if traffic allows.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical grid line so the sides do not lean. Keep the phone level and leave a little sky above the roof. For something different, try the corner of Las Vegas Boulevard and Hacienda Avenue for a diagonal view along the length of the building with the neighbouring tower beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the glass to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the gold glass keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. After sunset, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, about 30 to 60 minutes before sunset, or just after sunset.

text.access_note: The view from Las Vegas Boulevard is from a public street; for anything inside the resort, check the official site before you go.

name: Luxor Las Vegas
label: Luxor Pyramid
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Las Vegas Boulevard' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/27858544: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Luxor Las Vegas' (260 m across).
notes: Black glass pyramid with a sphinx.

text.description:
Luxor is a casino hotel at the southern end of the Las Vegas Strip, built as a 30-storey pyramid in an ancient Egyptian theme. It stands 357 ft (109 m) high and contains the largest atrium in the world by volume. Out front, a recreation of the Great Sphinx faces the Strip. It is about 106 feet high and 262 feet long. The resort opened on 15 October 1993, and a beam of light shines from the tip of the pyramid into the night sky.

It photographs well because the shapes are so simple. A dark, sloping pyramid, a big sign and a Sphinx sit in one frame, with plenty of sky around them. For the classic picture, use the sidewalk directly in front of the main entrance. You get the pyramid, the Luxor sign and the entrance together, shot from street level. If you want the pyramid and the Sphinx in one shot, a local guide suggests the walkway from the drop-off area. For a closer, wide view of the Sphinx with the pyramid rising behind it, try the Sphinx itself, though access there may be limited when the tram is not running.

Stay on the sidewalk and keep out of the road and the resort driveways. Photograph the outside and the lobbies only, as casino floors are often no-photo areas. Come back after dark if you can, because the light beam is a good night subject.
text.geographic_location: Luxor is at the southern end of the Las Vegas Strip, in Paradise, Nevada. It sits between Excalibur to the north and Mandalay Bay to the south.
text.directions_text: Luxor sits between Excalibur and Mandalay Bay, and the Mandalay Bay Tram links the three resorts. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the pyramid, the Luxor sign and the entrance together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move close to the Sphinx and want it with the pyramid behind. At night, try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the top of the pyramid and the light beam.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Las Vegas Boulevard (sidewalk directly in front of the Luxor main entrance, not in the road). The pyramid facade with the Luxor sign and the entrance, shot from street level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the sides of the pyramid straight, so the sloping edges don't look tilted. Hold the phone upright to include the sign and the full height of the pyramid, or turn it sideways to take in more of the entrance. For an alternative, walk the path from the drop-off area to fit the pyramid and the Sphinx in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pyramid to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky stays blue and the facade keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a solid rail. Lower the exposure slider so the light beam does not turn into a white blob.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Just after sunrise, when there are fewer people, according to one local guide. Check on the day, and also try after dark for the light beam.

text.access_note: The sidewalk on Las Vegas Boulevard is open public space, but the Sphinx area may be limited at times and casino floors are usually no-photo zones, so check the official site before you go.

name: The Venetian Las Vegas
label: The Venetian
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Rialto Bridge' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Rialto Bridge' (way/543638181): middle (65 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/7770314: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Venetian Las Vegas' (426 m across).
notes: Venice-themed resort with a campanile and canals.

text.description: The Venetian is a big resort on the Las Vegas Strip, themed after Venice, with copies of several of the city's landmarks. Out front you'll find a Venice-style Rialto Bridge and a Campanile tower, with the resort's facade behind them. That grouping is the reason it photographs well: you get a bridge, a tower and a long frontage in one frame, and the whole scene is easy to read in a phone picture. The resort opened on 4 May 1999 on the site of the old Sands Hotel and Casino, which was demolished in 1996. It began with a 35-story tower, and the later Venezia tower brought the total to 4,049 rooms. The Palazzo, a sister property, opened next door to the north in 2007. The resort also has a canal with gondola rides, but the Grand Canal Shoppes are indoors, so this spot is about the view from outside. Expect plenty of people through most of the day. Photo guides suggest going early in the morning if you want fewer people in the shot. Casual phone photos are generally fine, but check the official site before you go if you plan anything more elaborate. Take a wide shot first, then move closer for a tighter picture of the bridge and the tower together.
text.geographic_location: The Venetian sits on the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise, Nevada, just south of its sister resort, the Palazzo. The Rialto Bridge replica is at the resort's front entrance.
text.directions_text: The Rialto Bridge and Campanile replicas are at the front entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the bridge, the tower and the facade into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Rialto Bridge (replica at the resort's front entrance, next to the Campanile replica). The Venice-style bridge replica and the Campanile tower framed against the resort's exterior. From here the photo should show the bridge and the Campanile framed against the resort's exterior.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the Campanile up with a vertical line so the tower doesn't lean. If the bridge is in view, keep it in the foreground and let the facade fill the background. For a second picture, try the resort's Venetian facade reflected in the front lagoon, with the replica landmarks behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright so the building keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take a few frames, as people will keep walking through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is suggested for fewer people. The resort is busy most of the day.

text.access_note: The front of the resort can be photographed from outside, but check the official site before you go for any rules on photography or access.
claims_not_in_sources: The Campanile replica stands next to the Rialto Bridge replica at the front entrance.
The front lagoon can give a reflection of the facade, which works best when the water is calm.
Gridlines and a lowered exposure slider help keep a tall tower straight and a bright sky from washing out the picture.
The middle of the resort is about 2 minutes on foot east of the stand-here point.

name: Excalibur Hotel and Casino
label: Excalibur
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8086330: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Excalibur Hotel & Casino' (347 m across).
notes: Medieval castle-themed resort.

text.description:
Excalibur is a castle-themed resort on the Las Vegas Strip, and it is one of the easiest buildings on the Strip to recognise: stone-style turrets, a moat and drawbridge, and towers topped with red and blue roofs. It opened on 19 June 1990. Its designer, Veldon Simpson, took particular inspiration from Germany's Neuschwanstein Castle. The four 28-storey towers hold almost 4,000 rooms, and when it opened it was the largest hotel in the world, until the MGM Grand took that title in 1993.

For a phone photo, the best approach is a wider street-level view rather than a close-up. Stand at the corner of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue and look across the road. The castle towers fill the background and are reflected in the pool in front of New York-New York. That puts a famous castle, a reflection and a slice of the surrounding Strip in one frame, which close-ups at the castle gate can't do. If you want a tighter shot, the red-and-blue towers and castle facade with the moat in the foreground make a strong picture. Another option is a higher, off-street angle from the walkway that links the Excalibur to the Luxor. Check current access to the moat and walkways before you go, as these can change.
text.geographic_location: Excalibur is on the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise, Nevada, at the south-west corner of the Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue crossing. It sits opposite New York-New York, with the Luxor and Mandalay Bay further south.
text.directions_text: Head for the corner of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue on the Strip. Once there, walk to the New York-New York side of Tropicana Avenue and find the reflecting pool in front of the hotel. The Excalibur is then across the road to the south-west, with pedestrian bridges linking this corner to the surrounding resorts. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the towers, the road and the pool reflection in one frame. If you want just the castle without the traffic, switch to the default lens (1x) or a gentle telephoto (2x) and crop in on the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Las Vegas Boulevard and Tropicana Avenue (on the New York-New York side of Tropicana Avenue, at the reflecting pool in front of New York-New York). The Excalibur seen across Tropicana Avenue, with its towers reflected in the New York-New York pool.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the pool's edge on the lower line, so the reflection fills the foreground and the towers sit above it. Keep your phone level so the towers don't lean. For a different view, try the moat and castle facade at the Excalibur itself, or the higher walkway angle towards the Luxor.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the towers to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky doesn't wash out the colours. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone against a railing or your body to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening, once the lights are on, usually gives the most colourful result. Early morning is calmer for a clearer reflection in the pool.

text.access_note: Check access to the pool area, moat and walkways before you go, as it may change. The official site is the best place to look.
claims_not_in_sources: The castle's lighting is usually on in the evening, which makes colourful photos.
A calm pool surface usually gives a clearer reflection, and early morning is often calmer.
Resting a phone against a railing or your body helps keep night-mode shots steady.

name: The Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas
label: The Cosmopolitan
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'The Chandelier' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'The Chandelier' (node/1737961737): point; moved 35 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/134795273: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Cosmopolitan of Las Vegas' (74 m across).
notes: Modern twin-tower resort next to the Bellagio fountains.

text.description:
The Cosmopolitan is a large resort casino and hotel on the Las Vegas Strip, and its best-known photo spot is indoors: the hanging crystal chandelier. From the second-floor railings you look across at the chandelier, with the glittering strands filling the background. You can then put a friend or family member in front of it. The railings run along a good stretch of the floor, so several people can take pictures without all crowding one spot.

The resort opened on 15 December 2010 and, at a cost of $3.9 billion, was the most expensive resort built on the Strip up to that point. It has two towers with 3,033 rooms, and a casino of around 100,000 square feet. The site is only 8.5 acres, which is small for a Strip resort, so the builders went upwards rather than outwards. Separately, the retail, restaurants and pools are on the second and third floors.

This is a view of the interior, not a view of the building's outside. If you want the exterior, there is no free public viewing spot we can point you to. The Las Vegas Boulevard pavement shows the Bellagio fountain field diagonally, but the Cosmopolitan is only at the edge of that frame.

Expect crowds around the chandelier. Take a few frames, step aside, and let others in. Keep your phone strap round your wrist while leaning near the railing.
text.geographic_location: The Cosmopolitan stands on the Las Vegas Strip, just south of the Bellagio and its fountains. The chandelier is inside the casino resort, on the second floor.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground, tram or rail stops listed for this spot. The Cosmopolitan is on the Las Vegas Strip, just south of the Bellagio. Once inside, head up to the second floor and find the railings facing the chandelier. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole chandelier and the railings around it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a friend in front. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for close detail of the crystal strands.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (second-floor railings inside the casino, facing the hanging crystal chandelier). The Cosmopolitan's glass-crystal chandelier as a backdrop, with people or a friend framed in front of the railings.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the railing level along a grid line so the picture looks tidy. Place your friend off-centre and let the chandelier glow behind them. For a different angle, walk a little way along the railings. The pavement on Las Vegas Boulevard is an alternative if you want the Bellagio fountain field instead, though the Cosmopolitan will only be at the edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on your friend's face to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright chandelier does not wash out. Portrait mode works well for a person in front of it. If the phone offers night mode in the dim light, hold still for the second or two it needs.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No best time is given for this spot. Because it is inside a hotel, check the hotel's access rules on the official site before you go.

text.access_note: The chandelier is inside a hotel and casino, so access rules may apply; check the official site before you go.

name: The Strat
label: The Strat Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/135456188: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Strat' (423 m across).
notes: Tallest observation tower in the US, with an observation deck.

text.description:
The Strat is a hotel and casino resort on Las Vegas Boulevard, built around a tall observation tower. It opened in 1996 as the Stratosphere and took its current name in January 2020. The tower stands 1,149 feet (350 m) tall, the tallest observation tower in the United States. At the top, a pod holds a revolving restaurant, lounges, observation decks and several thrill rides. The hotel, casino, showroom and shopping mall sit at its base.

The tower photographs well because it is simple and very tall. It rises from a low resort, so there is plenty of empty sky around the slim shaft and the pod on top. The story behind it is a good one too. Bob Stupak first planned it as a giant neon sign for his Vegas World casino, and it grew into an observation tower. The height was a battle, because the aviation authorities objected to the taller versions he proposed.

The phone icon on the map is in the middle of the resort, so you will be right at the foot of the tower. That means a dramatic upward shot, with the shaft narrowing towards the pod. For a calmer picture, walk back across the car parks and roads around the resort until the whole tower fits in the frame. Keep your phone upright and level, and use the gridlines to keep the shaft straight. Watch for reflections if you shoot through glass.
text.geographic_location: The Strat is on Las Vegas Boulevard, just north of the Las Vegas Strip and south of downtown Las Vegas. It is within the city limits rather than in the main Strip resort area.
text.directions_text: The easiest way is by taxi from the northern end of the Las Vegas Strip or from downtown Las Vegas. Ask for The Strat on Las Vegas Boulevard. The tower is visible from a long way off, so you can steer by it as you approach. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of the tower in when you are close. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched view from further back. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the pod at the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Look up and shoot the shaft from base to pod.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the shaft up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Hold the phone upright and keep it level. Leave some sky above the pod. A foreground such as a palm tree, a lamp or the edge of a building adds depth and scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the tower does not wash out. Use night mode after dark and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the sky is clearer and the light is softer. Dusk, when the tower is lit against a darkening sky, also works well.

text.access_note: The area around the resort is a working hotel and casino, and the tower's observation deck and rides are likely to be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

photo.artist: Original uploader was Timjarrett at en.wikipedia

name: Fountains of Bellagio
label: Bellagio Fountains
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Las Vegas Boulevard' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/22971030: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Fountains of Bellagio' (350 m across).
notes: Choreographed water show on the lake in front of the Bellagio.

text.description:
The Fountains of Bellagio are a free water show on the Las Vegas Strip, performed on an 8.5-acre man-made lake in front of the Bellagio resort. Jets of water move in time to music, lit by 4,792 white lights, and the tallest shooters can throw water as high as 460 feet (140 m). The show opened with the resort on 15 October 1998, on the site of the old Dunes hotel-casino, and it is often described as one of the most photographed places in the United States.

It photographs well because everything is in one frame: moving water, a long lake and the Bellagio facade behind it. The classic shot is straight-on from the Las Vegas Boulevard sidewalk, right at the lake's railing, and it is the most recognisable Las Vegas picture you can take for free. The railing is busy, so arrive early to claim a place. If you want a different view, try the pedestrian bridge over the boulevard for a higher, wider angle with the Strip's neon behind, or the east side of the boulevard, where the Paris Las Vegas Eiffel Tower can fit into the same frame.

Shows usually run every half hour from the afternoon until midnight, and more often after dusk, so timing varies with the season. Aim for the first show after sunset, when the sky is still blue and the lights are fully on. Weekend evenings are the most crowded.
text.geographic_location: On the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise, Nevada, on the lake in front of the Bellagio resort. The best-known viewing place is the west sidewalk of Las Vegas Boulevard, along the Bellagio frontage.
text.directions_text: There is no Underground, tram or similar stop at this spot, so head for the Bellagio on the Las Vegas Strip. Go to the west sidewalk of Las Vegas Boulevard, in the middle of the Bellagio frontage, and walk to the lake's railing. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole lake and the hotel facade in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a tidier, less stretched look. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for single jets and the lights on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Las Vegas Boulevard (west sidewalk, centre of the Bellagio frontage, at the lake's railing). The full fountain display with the Bellagio facade behind it, the classic straight-on postcard frame. The fountains spread out to the west in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the line of the lake edge level. Put the water in the lower half and the hotel facade above it. Hold the phone steady against the railing if you can. For a different view, try the pedestrian bridge for a higher, wider angle, but check its name on the map before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright jet to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lights do not wash out. Try Live Photos or a short video to catch the movement. Night mode can soften the water, so check the result and switch it off if the jets look smeared.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, at the first show after sunset, when the sky is still blue and the fountain lights are fully on. Arrive early, because the railing fills up, especially on weekend evenings.

text.access_note: The show is free and watched from the public sidewalk, but show times vary and it can be cancelled in strong wind, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens (0.5x) should be wide enough to fit the whole lake and the hotel facade from the railing.
Lowering the exposure slider helps stop bright fountain lights from washing out on a phone.
Night mode can soften or smear moving water.

name: Fremont Street Experience
label: Fremont Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fremont Street and Las Vegas Boulevard intersection' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Fremont Street and Las Vegas Boulevard (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Fremont Street Experience'.
notes: Covered pedestrian mall with a huge LED canopy.

text.description:
Fremont Street Experience is the pedestrian mall at the heart of downtown Las Vegas, and its big draw is a huge arched canopy over the street. The canopy is about 27 m high at the peak and runs for four blocks, roughly 419 m. Its underside is a giant LED screen. The light show opened in December 1995 with incandescent lighting, and the LED display came with a major upgrade in 2004 that brought in a 12.5-million-LED display. A further renovation began in 2019. Before each show, the lights on the buildings underneath are switched off, so the screen takes over the street.

It photographs well because everything is close together: the canopy overhead, neon casino fronts on both sides and plenty of people for scale. A horse-and-rider neon sign from the old Hacienda hotel-casino was placed near this entrance in 1996. The diagonal crosswalk here puts you in the middle of the junction, with the Fremont East sign, a vintage neon martini glass and a red Silver Slipper sign around you. The full canopy view is a short walk north-west along the mall.

For a different angle, the top level of the Binion's parking garage looks down on the Fremont Street marquee and the street below. Check that it is open before you go. Expect crowds, and keep your phone in hand rather than set down, as tripods are reportedly not allowed on the mall.
text.geographic_location: In downtown Las Vegas, on the westernmost five blocks of Fremont Street.
text.directions_text: There are no public transport stops listed for this spot, so get to downtown Las Vegas by taxi or rideshare, or on foot, and ask for the junction of Fremont Street and Las Vegas Boulevard. From there the main canopy lies to the north-west, about 350 m on foot along the pedestrian mall. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: At the crosswalk, use the default lens (1x) for the signs and the person in the junction. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) once you are under the canopy to fit the arch and the casino fronts into one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Fremont Street and Las Vegas Boulevard (the diagonal crosswalk in the middle of the intersection). The Fremont East sign, a vintage neon martini glass and a red Silver Slipper sign framing a person standing in the intersection. The canopy and the main mall lie to the north-west. Only step onto the crosswalk when the signal allows.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place your subject on one of the lines, with the neon signs on either side. Ask a friend to stand in the middle of the junction, as the signs frame them well. Then walk north-west and shoot along the mall with ultra-wide, keeping the arch of the canopy symmetrical. For another angle, try the top level of the Binion's parking garage, looking down the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright sign to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the neon colours stay rich and don't wash out. Under the canopy, try a Live Photo to catch the changing lights, or use night mode and hold still for a sharper shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the neon and the canopy lights are at their best. Weekend nights are especially crowded, so go earlier in the evening if you want more space.

text.access_note: The mall is a public pedestrian street, but check the official site before you go for show times, current photo rules and whether the Binion's garage top level is open.

name: Mob Museum
label: The Mob Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/206128504: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'The Mob Museum' (59 m across).
notes: Organized crime museum in the old downtown courthouse.

text.description:
The Mob Museum sits in the former Las Vegas Post Office and Courthouse, a solid civic building from 1933 that is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Today it is a history museum about organised crime in the United States and the efforts of law enforcement to stop it. It opened on 14 February 2012 on Stewart Avenue, two blocks north of Fremont Street in Downtown Las Vegas.

It photographs well because it looks quite different from the neon casinos nearby. The building is a formal, historic piece of architecture, and that contrast gives you a good 'old Las Vegas' frame. The exterior is the easy shot for a phone: stand back far enough to get the whole frontage, then move in for details such as the entrance and the stonework.

A few facts help you tell the story in a caption. The second-floor courtroom, which hosted one of the fourteen national Kefauver Committee hearings on organised crime held in 1950 and 1951, is the museum's centrepiece. The museum also displays the brick wall from the Saint Valentine's Day Massacre. The city bought the old post office and courthouse in 2000 on condition that it was restored and put to cultural use.

Inside, photography rules may vary from room to room, so ask staff or check the museum's guidance before you shoot. For a quick, free picture, the outside of the building gives you the best view.
text.geographic_location: In Downtown Las Vegas, on Stewart Avenue, about two blocks north of Fremont Street and the downtown casino district.
text.directions_text: The museum is on Stewart Avenue in Downtown Las Vegas, two blocks north of Fremont Street. Look for the large old courthouse building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you cannot step back far enough. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for doorway and stonework details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the whole frontage, step back from the building along the pavement until it fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the vertical edges of the building up with them so the walls do not lean. Keep the entrance in the centre or on one third line, and include a little pavement for scale. Take one wide shot, then one close shot of a detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out the stonework. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a post or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daytime gives clear, even light on the frontage. Early evening can add the glow of the street lights and signs, which works well with night mode.

text.access_note: The museum is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for opening times, tickets and photography rules; the outside can be photographed from the street.
claims_not_in_sources: The exterior of the building can be photographed from the public pavement without a ticket.
Photography rules inside the museum may vary from room to room.
The pavement outside the museum is narrow enough that the ultra-wide lens may help.
Daytime light on the frontage is even, and street lighting and signs add a glow in the early evening.

name: Neon Museum
label: Neon Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'La Concha Motel lobby' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'La Concha Motel Sign' (pois).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6993430 (coordinate location).
notes: Outdoor collection of vintage Las Vegas signs.

text.description: The Neon Museum is an outdoor collection of retired Las Vegas signs from old casinos, motels and shops, spread over about 2.27 acres. For a phone photographer there are two quite different pictures here. The first is the La Concha Motel lobby, a restored shell-shaped building with a sweeping curved roof. It was donated to the museum in 2005, cut into eight pieces and moved about 3.5 miles north from the Strip in 2006. It is now the visitor centre, and guides often call it one of the most photographed features on site. It makes a calm, architectural shot that stands apart from the crowded sign yard. The second picture is the Neon Boneyard, where rows of leaning, stacked and retired signs, such as the Silver Slipper and Huntridge, line a gravel walkway. The museum opened to the general public on 27 October 2012, and the collection now runs to more than 200 signs. For the lobby, step back until the whole curve of the roof sits inside the frame, and keep the phone level so the lines look natural. In the yard, look for a single sign against a clear patch of sky, or a long view down the walkway with signs leaning in from both sides. Entry is by paid ticket and only personal phone snapshots are allowed, so a phone is the right tool for the visit. Rules and plans can change, including the museum's announced move to a larger site, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Neon Museum is in downtown Las Vegas, on North Las Vegas Boulevard just north of Fremont Street and close to Cashman Field. It is away from the Strip, on the downtown side of the city.
text.directions_text: No Underground-style stations or tram stops are listed for this spot, so start from the Fremont Street area downtown and go north along North Las Vegas Boulevard by taxi or hired scooter. From there the main sign yard is about 3 minutes on foot to the north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole La Concha lobby roof, and the default lens (1x) for the sign-filled walkway. In the yard, the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for picking out one sign's lettering or lights without leaning over the barriers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at La Concha Motel lobby. The restored shell-shaped Googie lobby with its curved roofline, framed as a standalone architectural shot. Its curved roofline is the subject, so keep a little distance and let the whole sweep of the roof fit in. The sign yard, the main subject of the museum, lies to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the lobby's edges up with them, so the building does not lean. Keep the shot architectural, with few people in it. If you want something busier, the Neon Boneyard is the alternative: frame the leaning and stacked signs along the gravel walkway, and use a close sign as a foreground with others fading behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the lobby's roof edge, then nudge the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright. In the yard at dusk, tap on a lit sign and lower the exposure so the colours stay rich. Night mode can help once it gets dark, but rest your elbows on something steady. Only phone snapshots are allowed, so leave cameras, tripods and selfie sticks behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: The lobby suits soft daylight, and the Boneyard is at its best around dusk, when lit and unlit signs sit together. Evening visits are ticketed too, so check the official site for current times.

text.access_note: Ticketed site with paid daytime and evening entry, and only personal phone snapshots allowed; check the official site (neonmuseum.org) for current hours and rules before you go.

name: High Roller (Ferris wheel)
label: High Roller
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'LINQ Promenade' (4 web pages); placed at the stretch of LINQ Promenade nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/402543930: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'High Roller' (134 m across).
notes: Giant observation wheel at the LINQ Promenade.

text.description:
The High Roller is a giant observation wheel on the Las Vegas Strip, and it is one of the easiest big landmarks to fit into a phone photo from the street. It stands 167.6 metres tall and opened in March 2014 as the world's tallest Ferris wheel. Since October 2021 it has been the second tallest, behind Ain Dubai. It is the centrepiece of The LINQ development, and several guides recommend the LINQ Promenade beside it as an easy, free spot for photographing it.

The wheel photographs well because it is so big and so regular. The thin rim, the spokes and the row of glass cabins make a strong pattern, and walking closer lets you fill the frame with them. There are 28 cabins, each holding up to 40 people, so you can see the little capsules spaced round the rim. After dark about 2,000 LEDs light the wheel in solid colours or moving patterns, and that is when it looks best. The colours change, so take a few frames.

Use the default lens (1x) or the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to get the whole rim in. If you want a close-up, looking-up view, walk to the base of the wheel on the LINQ Promenade. If you want a tidier shot, try the quieter corner of the promenade behind the In-N-Out, where fewer people walk through the frame. Wipe your lens before you shoot, as city air and fingers leave smears that show up as glare around the lights.
text.geographic_location: On the Las Vegas Strip in Paradise, Nevada, on Las Vegas Boulevard across from Caesars Palace. The wheel is the centrepiece of The LINQ, and the LINQ Promenade runs between the Flamingo and The LINQ near the wheel's base.
text.directions_text: It is easy to reach on foot from the Strip near Caesars Palace and the Flamingo. The wheel is on Las Vegas Boulevard, beside the monorail. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From where you stand, use the default lens (1x) or the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to show the whole wheel. Once you have walked to the base, switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the rim and spokes in and look up at the wheel. Use the default lens (1x) from further back for a calmer, less stretched view. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a few cabins against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on LINQ Promenade (ground level near the wheel's base, between the Flamingo and The LINQ, facing the wheel). The High Roller rising behind you or looming above from below, with the wheel's rim and spokes filling the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the wheel's centre near the middle of the frame so the circle looks even. Tilting the phone up, as you will at the base, makes the vertical lines lean inwards, so keep the phone as level as you can or accept it as part of the look. For a quieter alternative, try the corner of the promenade behind the In-N-Out, which has less foot traffic in the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wheel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the LED colours stay rich and don't burn out to white. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or lean on a solid surface to keep the phone steady. Try a Live Photo to catch the lights changing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset through blue hour, when the wheel's LED colours come on. One guide suggests about 6-8pm. Check the wheel's hours on the day.

text.access_note: The LINQ Promenade is an open public walkway, but riding the wheel is ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Vegas Vic
label: Vegas Vic
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Vegas Vic' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q2511844: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Giant neon cowboy sign downtown.

text.description:
Vegas Vic is the big neon cowboy on the front of the old Pioneer Club at 25 E Fremont Street, in the heart of downtown Las Vegas. He went up in 1951 and is about 40 feet (12 m) tall. He was meant as a friendly, welcoming figure rather than a plain lettered sign, and he has become one of the best-known faces of the city. His hat brim lost several feet in 1994 so that he would fit under the curve of the Fremont Street Experience canopy, which is worth looking for when you frame him. His shirt has changed over the years too, and today it is red and yellow checks, from a restoration in 1998. The sign was refurbished and lit up again in 2023. He no longer waves or talks, so you are photographing a still figure. The building below him is now a souvenir shop.

The phone icon on the map is directly beneath the sign on the Fremont Street side, so you are looking straight up at him. That low angle makes him tower over you, with the full glow of the neon against the sky and the canopy. If you would rather show him in context, step back across the street, where you can fit his whole figure in with the busy Fremont Street scene around him. Keep your phone steady with both hands, and watch out for people walking through your frame, because this is a busy pedestrian area.
text.geographic_location: Vegas Vic is on East Fremont Street in downtown Las Vegas, on the old Pioneer Club building at the corner with First Street. He stands at the edge of the Fremont Street Experience canopy.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or station information is given for this spot, so start from downtown Las Vegas and the Fremont Street area and walk to 25 E Fremont Street, at the corner of First Street. The phone icon on the map is right beneath the sign, so there is no extra walk once you reach the building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you are right under the sign, because it fits the whole 40-foot figure and some of the canopy into one frame. From across the street, use the default lens (1x), or the telephoto (2x-5x) to pick out his face and hat without walking closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows a dramatic upward view of the neon cowboy with his full glow, framed against the sky and the canopy.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Tilt the phone upwards and keep the figure in the centre so he looks tall and strong. Switch on gridlines and use them to keep the sign's vertical edges as straight as you can. For a wider view of the whole figure with the Fremont Street crowds around him, move across the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright neon to set focus and pull the exposure slider down a little, so the colours stay rich and do not burn out to white. If you are shooting after dark, try night mode and hold the phone as still as you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Neon signs show their colour best once the sky has darkened, so dusk or after dark should suit him. The sign also looks fine by day, but the glow is less striking.

text.access_note: The sign is on the street front of a building on Fremont Street, so you can see it from the public pedestrian area, but check the official site before you go for any events or restrictions on the street.
claims_not_in_sources: Neon signs generally show their colour best at dusk or after dark.
Fremont Street is a pedestrian area that is crowded in the evening.
The sign can be photographed from the public street without a ticket.
